title: Ramanuja's Promise
hook: a young man arrives too late to meet his teacher, finds three fingers folded on the dead man's hand, and makes three promises
carry: every vedanta school writes on the same shared books
tomorrow: Indra keeps going back to his teacher for 101 years. what is he looking for?

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vedanta, salt in the water: tat tvam asi, you are that, heard three ways and ranked by none.

Here's a story Sri Vaishnavas tell about Ramanuja. Yamuna, the great teacher at Srirangam, is dying, and he's heard of a brilliant young man and sent for him. Ramanuja hurries to Srirangam. He's too late. Yamuna has died, and three fingers of his right hand are folded down. People say the teacher left three wishes unfulfilled. So Ramanuja makes three vows out loud, and one of them is to write a commentary on the Brahma Sutra. As he speaks, the story says, the fingers open.
screen: `TOO LATE TO MEET HIS TEACHER.` → `THREE FINGERS FOLDED.` → `THREE VOWS. THE FINGERS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Why would a dying teacher care so much about a commentary? Because of how Vedanta works, and it's a real teaching about Hinduism. Vedanta schools don't start new scriptures. They stand on a shared shelf that tradition calls the prasthanas, the starting points. The Upanishads, what was heard, shruti. The Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna in the Mahabharata, a text of what was remembered, smriti. And the Brahma Sutra, the short, packed lines that gather what the Upanishads teach and answer objections. Shankara wrote on the Brahma Sutra and the Gita. Ramanuja kept his vow and wrote his Shri Bhashya on the Brahma Sutra, and on the Gita too. Madhva did the same. That's how a school stands up: by showing its reading fits the shared texts, all of them, hard verses included. The Brahma Sutra says why early on. Brahman is known from the Upanishads because they all fit together around it. The texts aren't a pile; they're meant to agree. So here's what that means today. Hindus from different traditions, a Shiva temple, a Vishnu temple, an Advaita study circle, a Krishna temple, may describe God differently, and many still revere the same Upanishads and the same Gita. The Vedanta schools' arguments are arguments about how the same pages fit. Nobody wins by changing the subject.
screen: `THE STARTING POINTS.` · `HEARD, REMEMBERED, REASONED.` · `EVERY SCHOOL WRITES ON THE SAME SHELF.` · `DIFFERENT TEMPLES, SAME GITA.`

segments.voice: Let one line you love come to mind, a verse from the Gita, a bhajan, something an elder told you, and say it inwardly, slowly. Ask what's here you haven't seen before. Don't hunt for a clever answer. Stay, the way a commentator stays with a single line, and see what it shows you. If you pray, you can hold that line as an offering.
Vedanta. Today, its shared shelf: the Upanishads, the Gita, the Brahma Sutra, and every school showing how they fit. Today's word.
Your line: every Vedanta school writes on the same shared books. Different readings, one shelf. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1195 COUNTS.` → `EVERY VEDANTA SCHOOL WRITES ON THE SAME SHARED BOOKS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT IS INDRA LOOKING FOR?`

notes: The term prasthana-traya means 'three starting points'; the script avoids stating the count and the etymology. Confirm the framing of shruti, smriti and nyaya prasthanas.

Ramanuja wrote the Shri Bhashya and a Gita Bhashya, but no separate commentaries on individual Upanishads (his Vedartha Sangraha treats them); the script says only that each 'read the Upanishads closely'. Confirm.
Brahma Sutra 1.1.4 (tat tu samanvayat) paraphrased as the Upanishads agreeing in Brahman; confirm.
Classifying the Gita as smriti is standard but some traditions treat it with near-shruti status; a Keeper may want that noted.
